paragraphs: Why does a training algorithm favor one solution over another when a neural network can fit its data in many ways? This paper studies that question through stability: how an optimization procedure behaves near a candidate solution. The motivation is to connect the structure of the training data with the kinds of solutions that optimization tends to favor.

The authors introduce a common linear stability framework for studying stochastic gradient descent, random perturbations, and Sharpness-Aware Minimization. Their analysis focuses particularly on two-layer networks with ReLU activations. Comparing these procedures within one framework provides a way to investigate their different preferences without treating each optimizer as an entirely separate theoretical problem.

The central ingredient is a new coherence measure connecting data geometry with similarity between gradients. This gives the analysis a concrete link between the examples being learned and the local behavior of optimization. The contribution is a framework for explaining solution preferences; the abstract does not establish that SAM universally generalizes better, or that flatter solutions always produce better predictions.
neurips-2025-a-unified-stability-analysi.tldr: A shared stability framework connects data geometry and gradient similarity to the solution preferences of SGD, random perturbations, and SAM.

paragraphs: ReStraV detects generated videos by examining how their visual representations change over time. Its starting point is the perceptual straightening hypothesis: trajectories from real-world videos tend to become straighter when expressed in a neural representation space. The paper investigates whether departures from that geometric pattern can help distinguish synthetic videos from natural ones.

The method uses the pretrained self-supervised vision transformer DINOv2 to represent video content. It then measures temporal curvature and the distances between successive representations. These quantities describe how sharply the representation trajectory turns and how far it moves. Statistical and signal descriptors summarize those measurements for each video, and a lightweight classifier learns to distinguish the resulting patterns.

The authors report significant differences between real and generated videos in both curvature and distance patterns. On VidProM, ReStraV achieves 97.17% accuracy and 98.63% AUROC, outperforming the compared image- and video-based detectors. The reported computational efficiency makes representation geometry a promising low-cost detection signal, with the demonstrated performance tied to the evaluations described.
neurips-2025-ai-generated-video-detectio.tldr: ReStraV detects AI-generated videos using differences in the curvature and movement of their neural representations over time.

paragraphs: This paper studies how stochastic gradient descent learns from sequences in a mathematically tractable setting. The authors introduce Sequence Single-Index models, where the prediction target depends on one direction in the input space applied across a sequence of tokens. The model family extends classical single-index models and includes simplified architectures with one attention layer.

The main analytical simplification is an exact expression for the population loss using just two sufficient statistics. These summarize semantic alignment and positional alignment, allowing the authors to characterize high-dimensional training through a small set of interpretable coordinates. This connects progress in optimization to whether the model is learning the relevant content and its sequential organization.

The analysis identifies two training phases: first escaping an uninformative initialization, then aligning with the target subspace. It also shows how sequence length and positional encoding affect learning paths and convergence speed. These results explain mechanisms through which sequential structure can benefit attention-based learning within the studied model family, rather than establishing a universal advantage for longer sequences or every attention architecture.
neurips-2025-asymptotics-of-sgd-in-seque.tldr: A tractable sequence-model analysis reveals two phases of SGD learning and how sequence length and positional encoding influence convergence.

paragraphs: Text-guided image editors can receive requests that do not make sense for the supplied image or that contradict one another. Trying to execute every instruction can then produce incoherent results. CAMILA addresses this problem by making the relationship between the image and the requested change part of the editing decision itself.

The method checks whether instructions are coherent with the image context. It is designed to apply relevant edits to the designated regions while ignoring instructions that cannot be executed. This connects language interpretation with the spatial scope of editing: deciding what a request means also involves deciding whether it applies and where the corresponding change belongs.

The authors construct evaluation datasets containing infeasible requests in both single-instruction and multiple-instruction settings. On these evaluations, CAMILA achieves better performance and semantic alignment than the compared state-of-the-art models while preserving image integrity. The findings support treating contextual validity as a core part of image editing, especially when a request contains several instructions that cannot all be meaningfully followed.
neurips-2025-camila-context-aware-maskin.tldr: CAMILA checks whether editing instructions fit an image’s context and applies relevant changes while ignoring infeasible requests.

paragraphs: In single-positive multi-label learning, an example may have several correct labels, but training reveals only one positive label. The remaining labels therefore contain unresolved information. This paper questions a common assumption used when assigning them pseudo-labels: that every category has the same underlying prevalence, even though real categories can occur at very different rates.

The proposed framework, Crisp, estimates these category-specific class priors and uses them to construct the learning objective. The authors provide a theoretical guarantee that their prior estimates converge to the true priors. They also derive an unbiased estimator of classification risk, connecting the estimated label frequencies to the quantity that the model is trained to minimize.

The corresponding risk minimizer is guaranteed to approximately converge to the optimal minimizer available with fully supervised data. That is an approximate convergence claim, rather than a promise of identical predictions with limited annotations. Experiments across ten multi-label benchmarks report improvements over existing single-positive methods, supporting the value of explicitly accounting for unequal class frequencies.
neurips-2025-can-class-priors-help-singl.tldr: Crisp estimates unequal class frequencies to improve learning when each training example has only one observed positive label.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning controller can perform well in experiments without having a mathematical certificate of stable behavior. This paper develops certificates from the controller’s value function. Classical Lyapunov certificates require a quantity to decrease at every step, a condition that can be difficult to establish for policies produced by learning.

The authors first analyze the linear quadratic regulator setting. They find that adding a residual term tied to the dynamics and stage cost can turn a policy’s value function into a Lyapunov function. They also use a generalized condition that requires decrease on average across multiple time steps, allowing more flexibility than strict decrease at each individual step.

For nonlinear systems, the method learns neural residual corrections to reinforcement learning value functions. It successfully certifies policies on Gymnasium and DeepMind Control benchmarks. A further version jointly learns controllers and certificates through a multi-step loss, yielding larger certified inner approximations of the region of attraction than the classical approach. These are certified regions of stable behavior, not claims of stability from every possible starting state.
neurips-2025-certifying-stability-of-rei.tldr: Learned corrections to RL value functions enable stability certificates that require decrease across multiple steps rather than at every step.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based purification tries to defend a classifier by cleaning an adversarial input before classification. Its rationale is that diffusion will move the input toward natural-looking data. This paper challenges that rationale, proving that gradient-based attacks can target the diffusion model itself and steer purified outputs toward adversarial distributions.

The authors attribute inflated robustness estimates to inaccurate gradients and evaluations that test only one random purification. DiffBreak provides a toolkit for differentiating through the purification process while removing gradient mismatches. The evaluation also accounts for randomness and the risk of resubmitting an adversarial example, showing that the apparent defense strength collapses when these factors are considered.

The paper then examines a stronger decision procedure: majority voting over predictions from several independently purified copies. This statistically grounded alternative offers partial but meaningful robustness improvements over classification from a single purification. However, the authors adapt an optimization method from attacks on deepfake watermarking to construct perturbations that also defeat majority voting. Their findings challenge purification’s viability as a defense even after improving its prediction protocol.
neurips-2025-diffbreak-is-diffusion-base.tldr: DiffBreak exposes weaknesses in diffusion-based defenses by correcting attack gradients and accounting for purification randomness and repeated submissions.

paragraphs: Attention with bias adds prior information to the scores that determine which inputs attend to one another. Although this is widely used in language, vision, and scientific models, the additional bias can disrupt the tightly coordinated memory access and computation that make FlashAttention fast. The paper targets that specific source of computational expense.

The authors establish a theoretical connection between FlashAttention’s optimal efficiency and the rank of the attention weight matrix. Building on that result, FlashBias uses low-rank compressed sensing theory to reorganize biased attention computation. It supports fast exact computation for many commonly used biases and fast, accurate approximation for more general bias formulations.

This distinction matters because the method does not claim exactness for every possible bias. Its implementation makes use of highly optimized GPU matrix multiplication. The reported results include a 1.5-fold speedup for AlphaFold 3’s Pairformer and more than a twofold speedup for biased attention in vision and language models without loss of accuracy. These findings show that incorporating prior information into attention need not forfeit the reported acceleration benefits.
neurips-2025-flashbias-fast-computation-.tldr: FlashBias accelerates attention with additive biases through exact computation for many common biases and accurate approximation for general ones.

paragraphs: Changing a face’s apparent age creates competing demands: the transformation must be strong enough to reach the requested age while preserving the person’s identity. Large age gaps and extreme head poses make that balance especially difficult. Cradle2Cane addresses the problem with two jointly trained passes built on few-step text-to-image diffusion models.

The first pass emphasizes age accuracy. Adaptive noise injection, guided by age and gender descriptions, controls how strongly the face can change. Identity preservation is deliberately weak at this stage to permit substantial transformations. The second pass denoises the transformed image using two identity-aware embeddings, SVR-ArcFace and Rotate-CLIP, to strengthen identity consistency while retaining age-specific features.

Separating these responsibilities gives the framework an explicit way to handle the age–identity trade-off within an end-to-end training process. On CelebA-HQ, evaluations using Face++ and Qwen-VL protocols report better age accuracy and identity consistency than existing methods. The authors also report stronger robustness on unconstrained face photographs, supporting the approach’s usefulness beyond the controlled test dataset.
neurips-2025-from-cradle-to-cane-a-two-p.tldr: Cradle2Cane first changes apparent age and then reinforces identity, improving both objectives in the reported face-aging evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper improves theoretical guarantees for two related prediction goals. Multicalibration concerns prediction reliability across multiple groups, while omniprediction seeks predictions useful for minimizing several losses. The authors study swap versions of these goals in both online learning, where observations arrive sequentially, and distributional learning, where sample requirements are central.

Their efficient algorithm achieves an l2-swap multicalibration error bound scaling as T^(1/3), up to logarithmic factors, against bounded linear functions. The guarantee holds both in expectation and with high probability. It improves on the T^(1/2) rate posed in the motivating open question. The result also yields T^(2/3) bounds for l1-swap multicalibration and swap omniprediction with convex Lipschitz losses, improving the previous T^(7/8) rate.

These online improvements translate into reduced sample requirements. Ignoring logarithmic factors, the stated bounds are epsilon^(-3) for swap omniprediction and epsilon^(-2.5) for swap agnostic learning with squared loss. For l1- and l2-swap multicalibration against linear functions, they are epsilon^(-5) and epsilon^(-2.5), respectively. The contribution is stronger efficient-learning guarantees for the specified function and loss classes.
neurips-2025-improved-bounds-for-swap-mu.tldr: An efficient algorithm improves online error bounds and sample requirements for swap multicalibration and swap omniprediction.

paragraphs: Local color editing in a 3D scene requires identifying the intended region and maintaining a coherent appearance across viewpoints. Existing radiance-field methods can struggle with object boundaries, consistency between views, and dependence on annotated data. KaRF tackles these problems through a weakly supervised framework for recoloring selected regions of a scene.

The framework has two stages: segmentation followed by local recoloring. Both use Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, and the system incorporates geometric information from neural radiance fields to support learning with weak supervision. The authors introduce a residual adaptive gating structure that combines these networks with residual connections, adaptive parameters, and gates to improve segmentation and refine the resulting edits.

KaRF also includes a palette-adaptive reconstruction loss intended to improve the accuracy of additive color mixing. These components connect the problem of selecting the right region with that of producing the intended appearance inside it. Experiments report substantial qualitative and quantitative improvements over many state-of-the-art methods, supporting the combined design for more precise local color editing with reduced reliance on annotations.
neurips-2025-karf-weakly-supervised-kolm.tldr: KaRF combines weakly supervised 3D segmentation and recoloring to improve local color edits and their spatial precision.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene in three dimensions from video requires more than recognizing what appears in individual images. This paper develops a multimodal language model that reasons about 3D spaces directly from video, without requiring additional inputs such as point clouds or reconstructed bird’s-eye-view maps. The aim is to extract useful spatial structure from the video itself.

The proposed VG LLM uses a 3D visual geometry encoder to obtain geometric prior information from video sequences. It combines this information with visual tokens before passing them into the multimodal language model. This gives the language model an explicit source of geometry-related information alongside its visual input, while keeping video as the source of scene evidence.

Experiments report substantial improvements on tasks involving 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. The four-billion-parameter model achieves competitive results against existing state-of-the-art approaches despite not requiring explicit 3D data inputs. It also surpasses Gemini-1.5-Pro on VSI-Bench. These findings support the usefulness of geometry-aware video representations for the evaluated spatial reasoning tasks.
neurips-2025-learning-from-videos-for-3d.tldr: VG LLM extracts geometric information from video to improve 3D understanding without requiring explicit 3D scene inputs.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to adapt a person re-identification model to a new environment containing visible and infrared images. The new data have no labels, and the original training data are unavailable. SVIP addresses this source-free setting by using knowledge retained in the pretrained model to guide adaptation across both the environment change and the imaging modalities.

Three components divide that work. Source-Guided Contrastive Learning keeps the original model frozen and uses its feature space as a reference for learning discriminative target representations. Residual Transfer Learning learns adjustments to those representations while preserving source knowledge. Structural Consistency-Guided Cross-modal Alignment uses reciprocal structural constraints to identify reliable visible–infrared pairs and align the modalities.

Together, these components provide guidance without requiring source examples or target annotations. The model supplies a reference for discrimination, while structural relationships help establish cross-modal correspondences. Benchmark experiments report substantial gains in target-domain performance and improvements over existing unsupervised visible–infrared re-identification methods under source-free conditions. The findings specifically support adaptation when only the pretrained source model remains accessible.
neurips-2025-learning-source-free-domain.tldr: SVIP adapts visible–infrared person re-identification models using unlabeled target data and knowledge retained in the source model.

paragraphs: MGUP studies how to vary update sizes among parameters during training. At each iteration, it gives a selected fixed proportion of parameters larger step sizes and assigns smaller, nonzero step sizes to the rest. This provides fine-grained control within layers while continuing to update parameters outside the more strongly updated subset.

The mechanism augments existing momentum-based optimizers and is designed to require little integration work. The paper applies it to AdamW, Lion, and Muon, producing an MGUP version of each. This makes selective updating a reusable addition to several optimization methods rather than a technique tied to a single base optimizer.

The authors prove convergence for MGUP-AdamW without weight decay under standard assumptions. That guarantee has a narrower scope than the full collection of proposed variants. Experiments covering masked autoencoder pretraining, language-model pretraining, and downstream fine-tuning report better or more stable performance than the original optimizers. The results support selective step-size allocation as a practical strategy for improving training, with formal convergence established for the specified AdamW setting.
neurips-2025-mgup-a-momentum-gradient-al.tldr: MGUP gives selected parameters larger updates and the rest smaller nonzero updates, improving or stabilizing several momentum-based optimizers.

paragraphs: Increasing scale in reinforcement learning from pixels can reduce performance instead of improving it. This paper investigates the architectural source of that problem. Its focus is the point where a convolutional encoder, which processes the image, passes its output to the dense layers that follow. The authors identify this connection as the main factor limiting scaling in their analysis.

They call this interface the bottleneck and show that previous algorithmic and architectural approaches implicitly act on it. That observation connects seemingly different remedies through a shared underlying target. It also suggests that addressing the connection directly may capture the benefit of more elaborate approaches without requiring their full complexity.

The proposed remedy is global average pooling, a simple way to aggregate the encoder’s spatial outputs before they reach the ensuing layers. The authors find it effective for targeting the bottleneck. The contribution combines a diagnosis of why scaling can fail with a comparatively simple architectural response, making the encoder-to-dense-layer interface a concrete focus for improving pixel-based reinforcement learning.
neurips-2025-mind-the-gap-the-challenges.tldr: The paper identifies the encoder-to-dense-layer connection as a scaling bottleneck in pixel-based RL and addresses it with global average pooling.

paragraphs: Mathematical modeling starts before there is a clearly defined mathematical problem to solve. It requires interpreting a real situation, choosing abstractions, and constructing a suitable formulation. This paper formalizes that broader task for language-model agents and introduces MM-Bench, containing 111 contest problems across ten domains from the 2000–2025 MCM/ICM competitions.

MM-Agent organizes the work into four stages: open-ended analysis, structured formulation, computational solving, and report generation. This decomposition makes model construction an explicit responsibility within an end-to-end workflow. The intended output includes both a formal treatment of the problem and a complete solution report, rather than only an answer to a supplied equation.

On MM-Bench, the authors report that MM-Agent outperforms baseline agents and achieves an 11.88% improvement over human expert solutions in their evaluation. Using GPT-4o, the reported cost is $0.88 and 15 minutes per task. Separately, MM-Agent assisted two undergraduate teams that earned Finalist Awards in the 2025 competition, placing in the top 2.0% of 27,456 teams. That result demonstrates use as a modeling copilot within human teams.
neurips-2025-mm-agent-llm-as-agents-for-.tldr: MM-Agent structures mathematical modeling into four stages and reports strong benchmark results and successful assistance to contest teams.

paragraphs: Few-shot relational learning asks a model to reason about knowledge-graph relations from only a small number of examples. Meta-learning methods aim to make adaptation to a new relation fast, but the paper identifies two weaknesses: learning relation knowledge in isolation and failing to use the local context specific to each task.

MoEMeta separates shared relational knowledge from task-specific information. A mixture-of-experts component learns global relational prototypes, allowing recurring patterns to be represented across tasks. A separate adaptation mechanism captures local context for the current task. These two components address different needs: generalizing from what relations have in common and adjusting quickly to what makes a new relation distinctive.

The combined framework is designed to balance transfer across tasks with rapid local adaptation when examples are scarce. Experiments and analyses on three knowledge-graph benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing baselines and report state-of-the-art performance. The findings support explicitly modeling both shared patterns and local context, rather than expecting a single undifferentiated adaptation process to capture both effectively.
neurips-2025-moemeta-mixture-of-experts-.tldr: MoEMeta combines shared relational prototypes with task-specific adaptation to improve knowledge-graph learning from few examples.

paragraphs: Federated clustering seeks groups in data held by different clients without exchanging raw records. Many methods combine local summaries tailored to a particular clustering model. The paper argues that these proxies can become unreliable when clients have different data distributions, while collaboration also creates opportunities for privacy leakage.

OmniFC replaces model-specific proxy aggregation with reconstruction of the global distance matrix, which represents relationships between samples. It uses Lagrange coded computing so clients share encoded data. The authors establish exact reconstruction and privacy guarantees, including protection under client collusion. This construction is described as naturally resilient to differences in the clients’ data distributions.

Working through a common distance representation separates the federated collaboration mechanism from a particular clustering algorithm. That provides a unified way to extend diverse centralized clustering methods to distributed data. Theoretical analysis supports reconstruction fidelity and privacy, while benchmark experiments report stronger robustness, effectiveness, and generality than state-of-the-art alternatives. The central contribution is preserving global sample relationships without relying on heterogeneous local model summaries.
neurips-2025-omnifc-rethinking-federated.tldr: OmniFC uses encoded client data to reconstruct global distances exactly, enabling privacy-preserving clustering across heterogeneous clients.

paragraphs: This paper studies allocation when agents arrive sequentially, resources are limited, and selection must satisfy fairness requirements across groups. An additional complication is that one agent may belong to several classes. The method explicitly addresses overlapping memberships rather than treating the arriving population as a collection of disjoint groups.

The algorithm first constructs a fractional solution using a set-aside mechanism that reserves resources to enforce fairness. It then turns that solution into actual selection decisions through randomized rounding. The key theoretical contribution is a lossless rounding scheme: the integral algorithm matches the fractional solution’s expected performance while preserving the fairness guarantees.

The expectation qualifier matters because the performance guarantee concerns the randomized algorithm, rather than requiring every individual realization to have identical performance. The paper also proposes a learning-augmented version that incorporates untrusted machine-learning predictions to improve the practical balance between fairness and efficiency. Together, these contributions connect fair resource reservation, implementable discrete decisions, and the possible use of predictive guidance in one online allocation framework.
neurips-2025-online-multi-class-selectio.tldr: A randomized reservation-and-rounding method preserves group fairness and fractional-solution performance in expectation when allocating resources online.

paragraphs: Reasoning about a chart or visual document requires connecting each reasoning step to what is actually visible. Text-only chains of thought can fail to make that connection, contributing to visual hallucinations and weak integration of image evidence. Point-RFT trains a model to produce reasoning explicitly grounded in corresponding visual elements.

Training has two stages. First, format finetuning uses 71,000 diverse visual reasoning problems with detailed, grounded step-by-step rationales. Second, reinforcement finetuning targets visual document understanding. The initial stage establishes the desired reasoning format, and the reinforcement stage further improves performance while using that visually grounded form of reasoning.

On ChartQA, accuracy rises from 70.88% for the format-finetuned baseline to 90.04%. Reinforcement finetuning using only textual chains of thought reaches 83.92%, so the reported comparison supports an additional benefit from grounding the reasoning in visual evidence. Point-RFT also shows stronger generalization on out-of-domain benchmarks including CharXiv, PlotQA, IconQA, and TabMWP. These results support grounded reasoning for the evaluated visual-document tasks.
neurips-2025-point-rft-improving-multimo.tldr: Point-RFT combines visually grounded reasoning examples with reinforcement finetuning to improve chart and visual-document reasoning.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the data a model is intended to handle. LogitGap approaches this after model training by examining logits, the model’s output scores. The paper argues that existing post-hoc detectors leave useful information in the relationships among those scores underused.

The method explicitly compares the maximum logit with the remaining logits to improve separation between familiar and unfamiliar inputs. It then refines this idea by identifying a smaller, more informative subset of scores. An automatic training-free selection strategy determines which logits contribute to detection, concentrating the scoring process on information that is useful for distinguishing the two input types.

The authors support the approach with theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations on both vision-only and vision-language models. They report consistent state-of-the-art performance across diverse detection benchmarks and scenarios. The contribution is a way to obtain a stronger detection signal from a trained model’s existing score relationships, together with a selection mechanism that avoids requiring additional training for that refinement.
neurips-2025-revisiting-logit-distributi.tldr: LogitGap detects unfamiliar inputs by comparing the largest output score with an automatically selected set of other informative scores.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order fine-tuning reduces memory use by estimating updates through forward passes instead of backpropagation. Its estimated gradients can be inaccurate, however, slowing learning and producing worse solutions. This paper identifies an additional asymmetry: estimation error is more damaging when applied to large weights than when applied to small ones.

Sparse MeZO uses that observation to apply zeroth-order optimization only to a carefully selected subset of parameters. The authors propose a simple selection scheme and a memory-optimized implementation of sparse masking. The selection is intended to improve optimization quality, while the implementation preserves the memory advantage that motivates zeroth-order training in the first place.

The reported implementation uses inference-level memory and can fine-tune LLaMA-30b on a single A100 GPU. Experiments show consistent improvements in performance and convergence speed over MeZO without added overhead. On RTE, the paper reports a nine-percentage-point absolute accuracy gain and a 3.5-fold speedup. These findings suggest that restricting which parameters receive noisy estimated updates can improve both learning quality and efficiency.
neurips-2025-sparse-mezo-less-parameters.tldr: Sparse MeZO improves forward-pass-only language-model fine-tuning by restricting noisy estimated updates to a selected subset of parameters.

paragraphs: State entropy regularization encourages diversity in the states a reinforcement learning agent visits. Although it has shown empirical benefits for exploration and sample complexity, this paper investigates its robustness guarantees. The focus is structured, spatially correlated changes, which arise in transfer settings and differ from the small, uncorrelated perturbations emphasized by many robust learning methods.

The authors characterize robustness under uncertainty in both rewards and transitions. Much of the analysis compares state entropy with policy entropy regularization, which concerns diversity in action selection. This comparison separates the benefits of spreading behavior across states from those of making action choices more varied, showing that the two forms of regularization provide different advantages.

The theoretical account also identifies settings in which state entropy performs poorly, so the robustness result is not universal. Practically, its robustness benefits are more sensitive than those of policy entropy to the number of rollouts used to evaluate a policy. The findings therefore connect a particular kind of environmental uncertainty with both a regularization choice and its evaluation requirements.
neurips-2025-state-entropy-regularizatio.tldr: State entropy regularization offers robustness to structured environmental changes, with benefits that depend on the setting and evaluation rollouts.

paragraphs: Long-context language generation creates substantial memory demands, making attention approximation an important computational problem. This paper studies it in a streaming setting, where information must be handled as tokens arrive. The goal is to approximate attention while controlling the space required to maintain the information used in that computation.

The proposed algorithm, BalanceKV, selects a balanced collection of key and value tokens through a geometric process based on Banaszczyk’s vector balancing theory. Its guarantee concerns epsilon-approximation of attention. The core idea is to use a mathematically structured selection process to retain a collection whose combined contribution supports accurate approximation of the attention computation.

The authors also establish space lower bounds, complementing the algorithm with results about memory requirements for streaming attention. Empirical evaluations report improvements over existing methods both in attention approximation and in end-to-end performance on long-context benchmarks. Together, the theoretical and experimental results connect token selection, approximation quality, and memory complexity, showing benefits that extend beyond measuring the attention approximation in isolation.
neurips-2025-streaming-attention-approxi.tldr: BalanceKV uses vector balancing to select key and value tokens for streaming attention approximation with theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: WaRPAD detects generated images using pretrained self-supervised models without training a separate detector or requiring prior knowledge of the data. Its motivation comes from cropping and resizing augmentations used in pretraining: these teach models to produce consistent representations across differently sized views. The method turns properties of those representations into a detection score.

First, Haar wavelet decomposition identifies high-frequency directions associated with fine-scale pixel variation. A base score measures how sensitive the image representation is to perturbations along those directions. WaRPAD then rescales the image to a multiple of the model’s input size, divides it into patches, scores each patch, and averages the results to assess cropping robustness.

The authors evaluate real images spanning different resolutions and domains, alongside generated images from 23 generative models. They report competitive detection performance and strong robustness to test-time corruptions. They also demonstrate applicability across self-supervised models, connecting that portability to their common use of cropping augmentations during pretraining. Training-free here describes the detection procedure, which still relies on an already pretrained representation model.
neurips-2025-training-free-detection-of-.tldr: WaRPAD detects generated images without detector training by measuring pretrained representations’ sensitivity to high-frequency perturbations across image patches.
